sources.entry: Web Servers and Reverse Proxies. A web server is a piece of software and underlying hardware that accepts requests via HTTP (the network protocol created to distribute web content) or its secure variant HTTPS. summary.name: HTTP
summary.one_liner: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the application-layer request–response protocol that underlies data communication on the World Wide Web, as described in this Wikipedia article.
use_cases: learning how HTTP request and response messages work
comparing HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 behaviour
understanding HTTP methods and their safety and idempotency
reviewing HTTP caching and conditional requests
summary.what_it_does: This is a Wikipedia reference article describing HTTP, a stateless request–response protocol in the client–server model. It covers protocol versions 0.9 through 3, including how connections are reused in HTTP/1.1 and multiplexed in HTTP/2, and how HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. It explains message format, headers, and request methods such as GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, and PATCH, along with safe and idempotent method definitions. It also covers caching, byte-range serving, chunked transfer, authentication schemes, and HTTPS adoption statistics.
notable: Covers HTTP/0.9 through HTTP/3 with version history and status
Detailed table of request methods showing safe, idempotent and cacheable properties
Explains the transition from TCP to QUIC/UDP in HTTP/3
caveats: Primary coverage is HTTP/0.9, 1.0 and 1.1; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are covered in separate articles
Usage statistics on the page are point-in-time figures and may be outdated
